actions.fyi: Nothing needed from you. You caught the one bad call in this design and it is corrected; the next thing I bring you is pictures and a re-measure.

content.label: The air was never the problem
content.lead: Dense ground fog does not reach the sky at all. The assumption was that the sky is checked too coarsely; it is not.

blocks.alt: how far the sky's dimming lands from the right answer

blocks.text: How far the sky's dimming lands from the truth, 0 being perfect — same sky, same coarseness, fog the only difference, 440 times worse.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: The fog layer is a hundred metres thick and the sky is checked in kilometre strides, so the render steps clean over it.

content.label: Re-measured today, and nothing has moved
content.lead: Before designing anything I re-ran the yardstick on today's game. Every number came back identical to the ones this page was built on.

columns.name: How wrong the shipping fog is

blocks.label: The near air is not the easy half
blocks.text: I had assumed only the sky was badly wrong. The air between you and the car is 24% out on the glow as well, over fifteen kilometres and sixty-four checks. Both halves need the fix.

content.label: The fix, and it is smaller than the plan said
content.lead: Fog stops being sampled at points along a line and starts being solved for the whole line at once. The air keeps being sampled — it is smooth, and that is what sampling is good at.

rows: Checking a point every kilometre and hoping the layer is there
Solving the whole line of sight in one go
How much of the job was already done
The light coming through fog was already exact; only what you see of the fog itself was not

blocks.label: Why it collapsed to two
blocks.text: Nine of the ten places do not work fog out at all — they read a finished answer from the sky picture or from the near-air grid. Fix those two and everything downstream is fixed with them.

blocks.label: Patchy fog survives
blocks.text: Fog banks drifting in patches still work. The exact answer is applied over each stretch of the line rather than the whole of it, so the patchiness is kept and the accuracy is still won.

content.label: You caught a bad call, and it is corrected
content.lead: I had the sky and the near air solving fog differently — the sky in one go, the near air stretch by stretch. You said that breaks the very thing the job is for. You were right.

blocks.label: What I had wrong
blocks.text: Today those two agree at the horizon because they run identical code — they cannot disagree. My version would have replaced that guarantee with a test watching for it to break, and then asked you which order to manage the risk in. Inventing the risk was the mistake.

blocks.label: It also bought nothing
blocks.text: Solving the whole line at once and solving it stretch by stretch give the identical number — the formula is an exact answer read off the two ends of a stretch, so chopping the line changes nothing. The split was pure divergence for no gain.

rows: Sky and near air can disagree

blocks.label: The guard that stays, regardless
blocks.text: The yardstick currently checks the fog against a slower copy of itself. Change the fog and the yardstick changes with it, and it would go green however wrong the answer got. Today's fog is frozen as the thing to be judged against before a line of it moves.

items: The fog's own glow is not dimmed by the air it sits in, across a single stretch of the line. Small, and it gets a measured number rather than an argument.

The exact answer describes a flat fog layer on flat ground; a line of sight skimming the horizon is held at a shallow angle rather than curving with the planet. Every such line is already fully fogged, so it is invisible — but it is written down.

decisions.title: Build the exact fog first; re-measure; spread samples only if something is left over
decisions.why: Reverses the plan's stated order, where sample-spreading jumped the queue, and folds a third planned fix in for free. Approved 12 Aug.

decisions.title: The sample-spreading step is paused, not deleted
decisions.why: Its background reading is filed. If the re-measure shows anything left over, it is ready to build immediately.

decisions.title: How the exact fog combines with the air's own dimming over long distances is mine to design
decisions.why: The fog answer is exact for fog alone; the two have to be woven together along the same line of sight. This is the one genuinely unsolved piece.

decisions.title: There is no sunbeam feature — every light interacts with fog and air identically
decisions.why: Ruled 12 Aug and binding on everything downstream: no light may be shadowed in the fog while another is not, and a beam is not a feature, it is what a blocked glow looks like.

decisions.title: The fog's body privilege and the trackside lamps now have owners in the plan
decisions.why: Was written as 'the moon has no shadows'. It has them — the gap is that the fog asks the sun's slot regardless of which body is lighting the scene.

decisions.title: There is no sun and no moon — one kind of body, the same rules for everything
decisions.why: Ruled 12 Aug. Which body it is may be data — its disc, its phase, its colour — never a rule that gives one of them something the other cannot have.

decisions.title: The job is one way in for light, not a fix per kind of light
decisions.why: Ruled 12 Aug. Fog is handed the lights and applies one physics to all of them, so a source built later works by turning up — there is no separate job to add it.

decisions.title: Nothing places a celestial body by hand; the sky obeys the time and the coordinates
decisions.why: Ruled 12 Aug. A body's position is a result of when and where you are, never something you set. The hand-set sun and the switch that reaches it are deleted, so a scene, a test or a preset states a time and a place instead.

decisions.title: D3 is answered: fog is solved exactly over every stretch the render already walks, everywhere, with no exceptions
decisions.why: Dimming from two causes multiplies, so fog and air separate exactly: fog is the thin sharp one and gets solved outright, air is the smooth one and stays sampled. Revised 13 Aug on your call — the first version let the sky and the near air solve fog at different granularities, which would have broken an agreement at the horizon that is currently free. One rule, both paths, no seam to police.

decisions.title: Today's fog is frozen as the thing to be judged against, before anything changes
decisions.why: Otherwise the yardstick moves with the fix and passes whatever happens. This costs a morning and is the difference between a proof and a claim.

decisions.title: The two approximations the design leaves get measured, not argued
decisions.why: Both are small on paper. On paper is not a number, and this project does not ship one.

next.if_nothing: I freeze today's fog as the yardstick, then solve fog exactly in the sky and the near air with one rule, and come back with pictures and a re-measure.

steps.step: Freeze today's fog as the thing to judge against, and prove the freeze changed no number
Solve fog exactly over every stretch, in the sky and the near air alike; delete the sampled fog in the same change
Re-run the yardstick and the eight fog captures; report before and after, with the cost per frame
Decide on sample-spreading from that number, not from the plan
